newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr depressed, risks all on downside.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr depressed, risks all on downside.

text.p: The Australian dollar cowered close to key support at a thin midsession having been slapped down from atop 75 cents late Friday.
Traders said bids at US$0.7470 were holding the currency up at the moment but sentiment was poor and selling of AUD/yen out of Tokyo was piling pressure on, risking a break to US$0.7440.

A 0.5 percent rise in ANZ job advertisements for June reported earlier was too marginal the hve any immediate impact. But it did serve to support suspicions the official employment data for June on Thursday would not be strong enough to curb speculation of another official interest rate cut.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the local dollar was laid out at US$0.7475/80 having been knocked back from US$0.7519/24 late here Friday and a high last week of US$0.7573.
Resistance was seen at US$0.7530 and US$0.7550, the latter proved decisive in defeating all rally attempts last week, while support was expected at US$0.7390 should US$0.7440 crack.
It slid to 84.20/30 yen on the crosses from 85.15/25 as worries over Japan's ballooning trade surplus with the U.S. clobbered US$/yen to 112.60/70 yen from an early 114.10/15.
In trade weighted terms the local currency was down at 56.9 from 57.3 late here Friday.

The job ads data were the only domestic feature of note. The series has been extremely volatile recently as a record 16.7 percent jump in April was followed by a hefty 7.3 percent fall in May, making it hard to detect the message amongst the noise.

The essentially flat result for June did little to resolve the uncertainty and the trend estimate, while positive for the seventh successive month, showed growth slowed to 1.4 percent from 1.8 percent in May and 2.4 percent in April.
ANZ chief economist Saul Eslake estimated the data pointed to average jobs growth of about 13,000 month, which was barely enough to stop the unemployment rate from rising.
The correlation with the official monthly employment data, due Thursday, has not been high recently although the series have been as volatile as eachother.

Median expectations are for a rise of around 40,250 in jobs for June, which would almost exactly correct the 40,300 drop seen in May. It was that shock fall which first had the market scenting a fifth rate cut and it would take a much stronger gain this time to convice it otherwise.
"My line in the sand for jobs is 60,000," said J.P. Morgan senior economist John Kyriakopoulos. "That's the least it would take to make me reconsider the outlook for growth and rates."
His own forecast is for a rise of 30,000 in employment with unemployment stuck at 8.8 percent.

The May unemployment rate was only kept down by a sharp drop in the participation rate so there was a risk that if this bounced back to more normal levels in June the jobless rate could rise even if employment rose as expected.
Most analysts did not see the jobs data as a trigger for a rate cut, figuring the Reserve Bank was waiting for confirmation of the improving inflation background before moving.
This should come on July 23 and 24 when Q2 consumer price and wages data are released.
There has even been talk the headline CPI measure would show a negative result for the quarter -- implying deflation -- a prospect which has the debt futures market salivating.
